newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-German Gehe faces tough UK market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German Gehe faces tough UK market.

text.p: German group Gehe AG has opted to become a major player in a British pharmacy market just as the sector faces its biggest ever shake-up, analysts said on Monday.

The drug wholesaler and retailer would face a serious challenge in making its 684 million pound ($1.15 billion) purchase of the 900-strong Lloyds Chemists Plc chain pay off in an increasingly competitive environment, they said.

Earlier on Monday Gehe wrested control of Lloyds after a tough, year-long bidding war with British rival Unichem Plc, which sparked a review of the drug wholesale and retail industry by British competition authorities.
Gehe, which already controls around 38 percent of the British wholesale market, will emerge as a significant force in retailing after its victory.

Lloyds's outlets will be added to the 360 stores owned by Gehe's existing UK chain AAH, pushing it ahead of current market leader Boots Co Plc's 1,220 stores. Loser Unichem remains stuck firmly in third place with around 450 Moss chemists outlets.
But analysts said Gehe was paying a full price for Lloyds, particularly in view of the constant downward pressure on profit margins at Britain's 12,500 pharmacies.
Greig Middleton analyst Tony Cooper said: "All sorts of changes are starting to make pharmacies more of an interesting place, but not necessarily profitable."
According to analysts at Lehman Brothers, Gehe will be hoping to achieve annual cost savings of around 20 million pounds from the combination of the AAH chain with Lloyds.

The acquisition gives the group greatly increased power to negotiate discounts with manufacturers and other wholesalers, including Unichem, as well as savings from cutting out overlapping stores and closing Lloyds's head office.
But Gehe will also hope to ride a revolution in the way treatment is provided.

The British government, in line with health providers all over the world, is trying to push an increasing amount of drugs expenditure directly on to the public by boosting sales of over-the-counter (OTC) medicines.
In third quarter figures released earlier on Monday, retail giant Boots said its sales of OTC drugs exceeded prescription medicines for the first time ever.

There has also been growing speculation that chains like Unichem and Gehe will set up one-stop health shops under a planned liberalisation of Britain's National Health Service, combining doctor's services, minor surgery, chiropody, dental care and pharmacies under one roof.

But the opportunities are offset by intense competition, with Britain's powerful supermarkets believed to be considering similar moves. In addition Asda Plc, which has built up its own in-store pharmacy chain, has won government backing for a campaign to end the price-fixing system for non-prescription medicines, known as Retail Price Maintenance (RPM).
Even Marks & Spencer, home of the knitted cardigan and meal- for-one, is said to be looking at ways of putting the St Michael's brand name on items like vitamins and paracetamol.

Boots, which sells items from compact discs to kitchenware, can make up for margin pressures at its pharmacies. But Greig Middleton's Cooper said chains like AAH and Unichem's Moss are far more dependent on revenue from pharmaceutical dispensing.
"It is not easy to see where the profits will emerge three to four years on, especially with the ending of the RPM on OTC medicines," Cooper added. ($1=.5974 Pound)
